problem: LLM-planner zero-shot ObjectNav systems depend on cloud-scale LLMs such as GPT-4. Swapping in small on-device LLMs (LLaMA-3.2-11B, LLaVA-7B/34B) causes a large success-rate drop, because the small model cannot pick out the right sub-goal from a long textual navigation-map description. That growing map prompt also has a KV cache that exceeds device memory, and recomputing it at every planning step produces multi-second prefill latency.
motivation: On-device planning avoids cloud communication latency, privacy exposure and API cost, but a Jetson AGX Orin has only 32GB DRAM. Two observations drive the paper. First, the map prompt grows to thousands of tokens as navigation proceeds, and a small LLM's attention on the ground-truth best sub-goal decays with navigation steps (it gets lost in redundant map information). Second, reusing a prefix KV cache breaks as soon as map content is selected or reordered.
key_idea: Split the object-level navigation map into semantically coherent groups whose KV caches are computed independently, so they can be reused in any order. Group objects using the LLM's own early-layer attention. At each step, retrieve only goal-relevant groups with CLIP plus a memory-budget knapsack, which both fits device memory and prunes distracting context for the small LLM.
insight: The ablation (Table 4, LLaVA-34b) separates latency gains from accuracy gains. Discrete memory caching alone cuts real-time latency from 5.63s to 2.42s with unchanged SR (42.7→43.1). Attention-based clustering lifts SR to 63.3, and semantics-aware retrieval lifts it to 80.0 while cutting latency to 0.87s. So the small-LLM failure is mostly information overload, not capacity per se: pruning context helps more than a bigger model. Consistent with this, generic sparse-attention accelerators that only approximate full attention (MInference 35.3 SR, FlexPrefill 36.7) underperform even the full-attention planner. Replacing CLIP with an LLM for group selection gives only +0.7 SR at 7.5x the latency (6.55s vs 0.87s), so a cheap semantic filter is sufficient.
method: Modular ObjNav pipeline: Grounding DINO detects objects in RGB-D frames, and objects with 3D positions are stored in a graph/grouped navigation map. The LLM planner receives the selected groups, the goal category and the visited-object trajectory, and outputs 'The next subgoal is X at position (x,y,z)'. If the goal object is already in the map it is chosen directly; a lower-level controller then moves the robot to the sub-goal.

Discrete memory caching: each object group's KV cache is computed independently, with no cross-group attention, so caches are decoupled from group order and selection. Caches live in low-speed storage (CPU host memory on A6000, disk on Orin), and only the selected groups are loaded once per planning step. Newly detected objects are appended at the end of their group so existing KV is reused. Position encoding follows Prompt Cache (Gim et al.).

Attention-based memory clustering: existing groups plus newly detected objects are fed through only the first ~1/10 of the LLM layers, whose group caches are kept on-device. A new object joins a group if its average attention to that group exceeds a threshold; remaining objects form a new group. The first step's detections form the first group.

Semantics-aware memory retrieval: CLIP (~100M params) encodes each group's object text and the goal category, and the similarity is treated as the probability P_i that group i holds a promising sub-goal. Groups are chosen by a 0/1 knapsack that maximizes Σ(P_i − threshold)·x_i subject to Σ M_i·x_i ≤ M, where M_i is a group's KV-cache size and M the device budget.

Small-large model collaboration and cache locality: CLIP handles the easy pruning step and the LLM handles the hard sub-goal choice. Only groups with new objects are re-encoded each step, and adjacent steps tend to select overlapping groups, giving a high on-device cache hit rate that rises with memory budget.

numbers_note: The paper states only 'HM3D dataset' on Habitat. It gives neither the split nor the episode count, so the split is assumed to be the standard HM3D ObjectNav val. Baseline numbers in Table 2 appear to be copied from the original papers, which used different setups. On-device Jetson Orin latency (LLaVA-7b) and cache hit rates are reported only in figures (Figs. 1, 7, 9) without numeric tables, and no SR/SPL is reported for the 7b and 13b variants.
results: On HM3D ObjectNav, EfficientNav-34b (LLaVA-34b) reaches 80.0 SR / 41.5 SPL and EfficientNav-11b reaches 74.2 / 39.5. This beats the strongest zero-shot baseline, GPT-4-based LFG (68.9 / 36.0), and a naive LLaVA-34b MapGPT-style planner (42.7 / 21.0). On A6000, real-time planning latency falls to 0.87s (34b) vs 5.80s for a GPT-4 planner (6.7x), and end-to-end latency to 12.51s vs 59.34s (4.7x). Against vLLM the reduction is 6.5x (11b) and 5.1x (34b) real-time.
limitations: Simulation-only evaluation on HM3D with no real robot. The split and episode count are unspecified, and the low-level controller is not described. Baselines are copied numbers or the authors' own reimplementations, so comparability is unclear.
The 'on-device' claim is only partly demonstrated. The 34b headline result runs on 4x A6000, and the Jetson Orin is used only for LLaVA-7b latency, with no SR reported for it.

LLM planning is still far slower than small learned policies (stated limitation). The method depends on detector quality and on dropping cross-group attention, and success degrades under small memory budgets (74.7 SR at 16GB).
